key_insight: Fault transmissivity in granite evolves unevenly and episodically, while acoustic-emission activity tracks overall damage but does not consistently predict local hydraulic changes.
engineering_relevance: Spatially resolved hydraulic estimates can improve assessments of fault-controlled fluid flow where uniform permeability or acoustic-emission proxies may miss local variations.
method: Conduct a quasi-static shear-failure test in Westerly granite with fluid-flow and six internal pore-pressure measurements.
Invert measurements using a 3-D finite-element model to recover transmissivity in ten cells along the growing fault.
Compare recovered transmissivities with acoustic-emission counts, spatial density and amplitude-weighted activity.
evidence_signal: Synthetic ensembles yielded median mean recovery errors of 7–9%; experimental local transmissivities reached approximately 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ m³ and varied by a factor of 2.3 along the final-stage fault.
watch_item: Interior fault cells were less well resolved than the ends, and results from this laboratory test require validation before field-scale application.
paper_title: Heterogeneous and episodic permeability evolution and correlation with acoustic emission activity during faulting in granite
